paras: The Coenties Slip mob threat against Charles Uppher took place on 27 August 1900 in lower Manhattan, when a white crowd called for the lynching of Uppher, a Black seamen's boarding-house keeper, after he shot a white man. Police took him to the station unharmed, and the Sun called it "another race riot."

Uppher, aged 51, kept a boarding house for Black seamen and a shipping office at 26 Coenties Slip. He told the Sun that rivals envied him, among them James J. Galvin, a white Brooklyn boarding-house "runner"; police also suspected business envy.

By Uppher's account, Galvin insulted and struck him outside the building, then cut him on both hands with a knife and followed him up to his office. Uppher took a revolver, chased Galvin back to the street, and fired, hitting him in the mouth.

About 200 sailors and longshoremen, by the Sun's count, gathered and yelled "Kill the nigger!" while the Tribune heard references to the race riots and cries of "Lynch him." Uppher held the crowd off with his revolver until Policemen Turley and Mitchell and other officers got him to the Old Slip station.

Uppher was charged with felonious assault, and no arrests of anyone in the crowd were reported. The Sun called Galvin's wound "not necessarily mortal," but the Tribune said he was "quite low" before midnight. No report of Galvin's fate or of a trial was found.

The Tribune and the Sun ran separately written reports on 28 August. The Tribune's headline, "Crowd Menaces Negro Shooter," stressed that police saved the prisoner, and it called the crowd "rough characters hovering about the river front." The Sun headlined "Negro Mobbed by White Sailors," counted "two hundred whites to one black," printed the crowd's slur, and called Uppher "a hustler."
Der Deutsche Correspondent of Baltimore ran a German-language brief on 29 August crediting the police's prompt intervention with keeping the crowd off Uppher. No Black-press coverage was found.
The Sun put the shooting in the afternoon and the Tribune at night.

reader.title: Coenties Slip mob threat against Charles Uppher
bases: A white crowd called for Uppher to be lynched or killed after he shot a white man, and police took him away before it could act, so the episode is a threatened lynching rather than an assault (A1, A2, A3).
A crowd of about 200 called out "Lynch him" and "Kill the nigger!" after Uppher shot Galvin, but police took him to the station unharmed and no one was killed (A1, A2, A3).

The Tribune and the Sun printed separately written local accounts that agree on the shooting, the threatening crowd, and the police rescue, and a Baltimore German paper adds a third version (A1, A2, A3).

accounts.label: Uppher's account
accounts.gist: Galvin insulted and struck him, then followed him up to his office and cut him with a knife; he took a revolver, chased Galvin down to the street and fired.

accounts.label: Uppher on motive
accounts.gist: White men in the shipping business who were less successful were jealous of his prosperity, Galvin among them.

accounts.label: Police view
accounts.gist: Police believed business envy lay behind the shooting, since Uppher had recently won the hiring of crews for several shipowners in competition with Galvin and other shipping bosses.

framing.detail: The Tribune headlined 'CROWD MENACES NEGRO SHOOTER' and 'the police save prisoner from harm,' relayed Uppher's version, and called the crowd 'rough characters.'
The Sun headlined 'NEGRO MOBBED BY WHITE SAILORS,' called it 'another race riot' with 'two hundred whites to one black,' printed the crowd's slur, and called Uppher 'a hustler' and 'the negro.'
The Baltimore German daily ran a short New York item giving the self-defense claim and the police's business-envy theory and crediting police with keeping the crowd off 'the Negro.'

conflicts.note: The Tribune does not say only one shot was fired.
